The 19 year - old added 85 for the first wicket with Paul Horton ( 41 ) before Glamorgan claimed three quick wickets , two to teenager Lukas Carey . Dearden then dominated a stand of 90 with Mark Pettini ( 63 not out ) before being bowled by spinner Andrew Salter . Pettini steered the Foxes to a second batting point underneath the lights . Dearden , who was dropped on one , survived a couple of run - out chances in his lengthy vigil of 145 runs, an innings that anchored Leicestershire's first innings and set a challenging total for Glamorgan. His century, a testament to his resilience and growing maturity, included 18 fours and two sixes, played across more than five hours at the crease. It was an innings of two halves, patiently accumulating runs against the new ball before accelerating with Mark Pettini in a partnership that put the visitors on the back foot. The early scares, being dropped and almost run out, only seemed to steel his resolve, as he focused on building a substantial total for his team. His dismissal by Andrew Salter, a rare lapse in concentration, came from a ball that spun sharply back into him, ending a truly memorable individual performance.

With Dearden gone, Leicestershire still needed to consolidate. Mark Pettini, who had played an excellent supporting role, then took on the mantle of primary aggressor. He found an able partner in Ned Eckersley, and the pair continued to build on the platform Dearden had established. Glamorgan, despite their earlier breakthroughs, found it difficult to dislodge Pettini, whose experience shone through. Lukas Carey, though expensive in patches, continued to pose a threat with his pace and bounce, while Andrew Salter tried to tie down the scoring with his accurate left-arm spin. The Welsh county's bowlers, however, struggled to maintain consistent pressure as the pitch flattened out under the floodlights.

Pettini reached his own well-deserved hundred just before the close of play, guiding Leicestershire past the 400-run mark. They declared their innings at 415 for 7, giving their bowlers a brief spell at Glamorgan's openers before stumps. The declaration was a clear statement of intent, aiming to put Glamorgan under pressure immediately. Glamorgan faced a tricky 10-over period under lights, which proved challenging. Sam Northeast and Nick Selman weathered the initial storm, but the Foxes' new ball bowlers, led by Chris Wright, made them play at everything. Glamorgan ended the day on 28 for 1, having lost Selman cheaply, caught at slip off a superb delivery from Gavin Griffiths. Northeast (15 not out) and Marnus Labuschagne (8 not out) will resume tomorrow, with Glamorgan still trailing by a substantial 387 runs. The match remains finely poised, with Leicestershire holding a clear advantage due to Dearden's heroics and Pettini's late flourish, but Glamorgan will be hoping their strong batting line-up can respond on what appears to be a good batting surface. From Winston Churchill 's infamous visit to Belfast in 1912 to a 1963 Viking invasion re - enactment in a County Down fishing town , as well as tales of tourism , industrial heritage and sport , a dazzling mosaic of Ulster life is pieced together in unseen archive footage . Hundreds of unique films have been released to the public to view online for free after the British Film Institute ( BFI ) unlocked its archive as part of a major history project , From Britain On Film . Royal visits and Lord Mayor 's shows Royal visits and Lord Mayor's shows provide a glimpse into the formal public life of the region, charting the pomp and ceremony throughout the decades. Yet, the newly accessible collection delves far deeper, offering a profound window into the fabric of Ulster society. Beyond grand parades and political figures, viewers can witness the hustle and bustle of Belfast docks, the meticulous craft of linen workers, and the vibrant atmosphere of street markets. The everyday lives of ordinary people come to the fore, showing children playing, families enjoying seaside holidays, and communities gathering for local festivals.

This extraordinary collection, curated by the British Film Institute (BFI), spans over a century, chronicling moments of national significance, local customs, industrial shifts, and societal transformations. Footage ranges from early silent films of horse-drawn trams in city centres to post-war documentaries showcasing agricultural innovations in County Armagh, or the burgeoning tourism along the Antrim Coast. The films offer a living history of the province, illuminating the impact of major events and everyday life, showing a society in flux, adapting to industrialisation and evolving social norms.

Viewers can trace the evolution of industries, from ship-building in Belfast to intricate lacemaking. The development of infrastructure, towns, and rural life are all documented. Sporting events, from local GAA matches to international rugby, are featured, celebrating Ulster's sporting culture. These films are more than historical records; they are poignant time capsules, revealing the aspirations, struggles, and joys of past generations.

By making these hundreds of unique films available online, the British Film Institute (BFI) has preserved a vital part of the UK’s cinematic heritage and created an invaluable resource for historians, researchers, and anyone interested in Ulster life. This project truly brings to life a dazzling mosaic of experiences, offering unparalleled insights into a region often defined by its political narrative, but here presented through diverse lives and landscapes. From the serious to the whimsical, public spectacle to quiet routine, this archive invites us to explore the many facets of Ulster’s past, creating a comprehensive and deeply human record. The inclusion of early footage, such as Winston Churchill's 1912 Belfast visit, serves as a powerful reminder of how long film has documented significant moments in the region's history, contributing to this unparalleled visual compendium.

From Winston Churchill's infamous visit to Belfast in 1912 to a 1963 Viking invasion re-enactment in a County Down fishing town, as well as tales of tourism, industrial heritage and sport, a dazzling mosaic of Ulster life is pieced together in unseen archive footage.
Hundreds of unique films have been released to the public to view online for free after the British Film Institute (BFI) unlocked its archive as part of a major history project, From Britain On Film.
Royal visits and Lord Mayor's shows are documented in the collection, as is the tale of Churchill's appearance in Belfast when he addressed an audience of nationalists in Celtic Park and gave his support to Home Rule.
There are also dozens of travelogues that were used to sell Northern Ireland to tourists in Great Britain and the United States, helping to boost tourism in the years before the Troubles.
And in sport, the 1930 Ulster Tourist Trophy race held at the Ards circuit in County Down is captured on camera. The event attracted thousands of spectators and commanded the attention of the motorsport world.
The real gems, however, are found in the footage of ordinary people doing extraordinary things.
Films of people at work in the spinning mills and constructing the M1 at Stockman's Lane in Belfast shows Northern Ireland's industry at its booming best.
Another film captures the first time Northern Ireland hosted the World Ploughing Championships, and fittingly it is a local man who takes the title.
The colour footage from the 1959 competition in Armoy, County Antrim, shows Lawrence McMillan's crowning moment as he gets his hands on the Golden Plough.
But perhaps most revealing of all is a 1938 recording of the Royal Victoria Hospital in Belfast.
It gives a rare glimpse into the casualty department and operating theatres as they were then, 10 years before the foundation of the National Health Service.
While medicine has advanced considerably in the eight decades since then, some aspects of healthcare in Northern Ireland appear to remain unchanged - the film ends with an appeal from the chairman of the hospital's management board to reduce waiting lists.
Francis Jones, of Northern Ireland Screen, which gathered much of the footage, said the aim of the project was to preserve delicate film that could otherwise be lost.
"There is a pure nostalgia value to film. It's different to reading a textbook or history book," he added.
"To actually see the film has that kind of visceral appeal and really strikes a chord with people."
The full From Britain On Film archive can be viewed at the BFI Player.

Writing in the Journal of Aesthetic Nursing , clinicians say there is a growing trend for under-25s to seek the wrinkle - smoothing injections . But the research suggests " frozen faces " could stop young people from learning how to express emotions fully . A leading body of UK plastic surgeons says injecting teenagers for cosmetic reasons is " morally wrong " . Botox and other versions of the toxin work by temporarily paralysing muscles in the upper face to reduce wrinkling when people frown . Nurse practitioner Helen Collier , who carried out the research , says reality TV and social media are significant drivers behind this worrying trend. She observed that many young clients are influenced by the flawless, often filter-enhanced, appearances portrayed online and in popular culture, leading to unrealistic expectations about their own looks. Ms Collier, whose findings are detailed in the Journal of Aesthetic Nursing, expressed particular concern about the psychological implications of intervening with a developing brain's ability to express and interpret emotions. She explained that the muscles targeted by Botox are crucial not only for frowning but also for conveying a wide range of human emotions, from surprise to sadness. If these muscles are routinely paralysed from an early age, it could hinder a young person's capacity to fully experience and communicate their feelings, potentially impacting their social development and emotional intelligence.

The research highlighted that while older patients often seek Botox to reverse visible signs of aging, younger individuals are increasingly opting for "preventative Botox," hoping to stop wrinkles from forming in the first place. This shift in motivation raises profound ethical questions for practitioners. Ms Collier argues that genuine informed consent is difficult to obtain from teenagers, whose brains are still developing, and who may not fully grasp the long-term consequences of such procedures. She emphasized that the decision to undergo a cosmetic procedure like Botox should be made maturely, weighing the risks and benefits, something many under-25s are not yet equipped to do.

The British Association of Aesthetic Plastic Surgeons (BAAPS), a leading body of UK plastic surgeons, has echoed these concerns, reiterating its strong stance against cosmetic injections for those under 18, deeming it "morally wrong." Even for those slightly older but still under 25, BAAPS advises extreme caution and thorough psychological assessment before any treatment. They advocate for a focus on mental well-being and body positivity rather than promoting interventions that can have irreversible impacts on a young person's self-perception and emotional development.

Ms Collier's research, published in the Journal of Aesthetic Nursing, urges clinicians to prioritize the mental health and developmental needs of young patients. She calls for stricter regulations around the marketing and administration of cosmetic injectables to minors and young adults, suggesting that a mandatory cooling-off period and psychological evaluation should be standard practice. She believes that practitioners have a duty of care to protect vulnerable individuals from potential harm, and this includes resisting the commercial pressures to provide treatments that may not be in the patient's best interest. The findings underscore the urgent need for a societal shift away from the relentless pursuit of an artificial ideal of perfection towards embracing natural beauty and promoting healthy self-esteem among young people in the UK and globally. This involves educating both practitioners and the public about the true purpose and potential downsides of procedures like Botox, ensuring that informed decisions are made, and that the emotional and psychological well-being of young people remains paramount. The long-term effects of widespread Botox use in this age group on collective emotional literacy and non-verbal communication are yet unknown, adding another layer of concern for experts like Helen Collier.

Writing in the Journal of Aesthetic Nursing, clinicians say there is a growing trend for under-25s to seek the wrinkle-smoothing injections.
But the research suggests "frozen faces" could stop young people from learning how to express emotions fully.
A leading body of UK plastic surgeons says injecting teenagers for cosmetic reasons is "morally wrong".
Botox and other versions of the toxin work by temporarily paralysing muscles in the upper face to reduce wrinkling when people frown.
Nurse practitioner Helen Collier, who carried out the research, says reality TV shows and celebrity culture are driving young people to idealise the  "inexpressive frozen face."
But she points to a well-known psychological theory, the facial feedback hypothesis, that suggests adolescents learn how best to relate to people by mimicking their facial expressions.
She says: "As a human being our ability to demonstrate a wide range of emotions is very dependent on facial expressions.
"Emotions such as empathy and sympathy help us to survive and grow into confident and communicative adults."
But she warns that a "growing generation of blank-faced" young people could be harming their ability to correctly convey their feelings.
"If you wipe those expressions out, this might stunt their emotional and social development," she says.
The research calls for practitioners to use assessment tools to decide whether there are clear clinical reasons for Botox treatment.
Several assessment scales exist that take into account how thick the skin is, how sun-damaged it appears, and the depth of any wrinkles, but experts warn that some Botox clinics are putting financial gain first.
Ms Collier calls on therapists to spend time helping young people boost their confidence rather than reaching for injections.
She adds: "Though most of the effects of the toxin are temporary, research suggests the muscles don't fully recover from injections.
"We really need to understand the consequences of starting treatments too soon."
Dr Michael Lewis, a researcher in psychology at Cardiff University, says: "The expressions we make on our face affect the emotions we feel.
"We smile because we are happy, but smiling also makes us happy.
"Treatment with drugs like Botox prevents the patient from being able to make a particular expression and can therefore have an effect on our learning to feel emotions naturally."
Rajiv Grover, president of the British Association of Aesthetic Plastic Surgeons, says: "Injecting teenagers with Botox for cosmetic purposes is morally wrong and something that no ethical practitioner would do.
"This can only exacerbate body image issues at a vulnerable time."

This operation highlights the growing partnership between Colombian drug producers, particularly remnant factions associated with the dissolved Farc insurgency, and the sophisticated distribution networks of European mafias. This particular bust involved meticulous intelligence gathering over several years, a collaborative effort spanning multiple law enforcement agencies.

Authorities in Colombia and Italy, alongside Europol and other European police forces, executed synchronized raids following the DEA's lead. Among the arrests were key logistical managers in Europe and several suppliers in South America. The Farc commander arrested in Colombia was reportedly a crucial link, responsible for ensuring the quality and quantity of the cocaine supplied and facilitating its transport to coastal rendezvous points. Further investigations are underway in the region, including in areas near Santa Fe, where some of the preliminary processing and logistics for the illicit drug trade are suspected to have taken place, demonstrating the intricate web of this criminal enterprise. Andreea Cristea is the fifth victim of the attack on 22 March , in which Khalid Masood drove into crowds on Westminster Bridge then stabbed a policeman to death , before being shot dead himself . Ms Cristea , 31 , who was on holiday with boyfriend Andrei Burnaz , had been in hospital since the attack . It has emerged that Mr Burnaz had been planning to propose during the day out . A family statement confirmed Ms Cristea , who was an architect , had died on Thursday . The architect, who had been visiting London from Romania, was thrown into the River Thames during the rampage by Khalid Masood. She was rescued from the water but had suffered catastrophic head injuries and a severe lung infection, remaining in critical condition for weeks at St Thomas' Hospital. Her family, including her parents and sister, had maintained a constant vigil at her bedside, desperately hoping for her recovery, until her tragic passing.

Mr Burnaz, who sustained a fractured foot in the attack and has since undergone surgery, has spoken emotionally about the terrifying moments after they were hit and his desperate search for Andreea amidst the chaos. He described seeing Ms Cristea disappear into the water after being struck by the vehicle, and his frantic efforts to locate her before she was pulled out by rescuers. The couple, originally from Constanța, Romania, were on a romantic trip, and the revelation that Mr Burnaz had intended to propose adds a profoundly tragic layer to their story, highlighting the dreams and future abruptly stolen by the act of terror.

Ms Cristea's death tragically brings the total number of fatalities directly resulting from Khalid Masood's attack to five. The other victims were US tourist Kurt Cochran, retired window cleaner Leslie Rhodes, and mother-of-two Aysha Frade, all of whom were struck on Westminster Bridge, along with PC Keith Palmer, the brave officer stabbed to death by Masood at the gates of the Palace of Westminster. The attack, which stunned the world, transformed a bustling London landmark into a scene of unimaginable horror and grief.

Tributes have poured in for Andreea, remembering her as a vibrant, talented architect with a promising future. The Romanian Ambassador to the UK expressed deep sorrow, conveying the shared grief of the Romanian community for her loss. Her tragic passing is a stark reminder of the global reach of such violence, impacting individuals from diverse backgrounds who were simply enjoying a day out in a major capital. The investigation into Masood’s motives and potential associates continues, but the devastating human cost of his actions, epitomized by Ms Cristea and Mr Burnaz, remains the most poignant legacy. London, a city known for its enduring spirit and resilience, mourns its lost, but remains united against the hatred that seeks to divide it.

Manus Island was first opened in 2001 , and along with Australia 's other offshore processing centres , has played a central role in Australia 's controversial asylum policy . Papua New Guinea 's high commissioner to Australia, Charles Lepani, has indicated that the closure of the Manus Island detention centre will be a gradual process, emphasizing collaboration with Australia for the humane resettlement of the asylum seekers currently housed there. The Supreme Court ruling has put both nations in a challenging position, requiring careful diplomacy to resolve complex human rights and political issues. Lepani stressed that while Papua New Guinea respects the court's decision, the welfare of the detainees remains paramount. The Wales centre - like Halfpenny - is currently out of action after surgery.
Williams is already on a dual contract, which runs out in the summer of 2016.
"I know he's contracted until the end of the season and hopefully we'll get some rugby out of him in that time," said Pivac.
"There's lots of things happening behind the scenes at the moment and I'm not really in a position to give you anything that hasn't already been given out in a press release.
"Scott is our vice captain, one of leaders so we certainly don't want him going anywhere."

Halfpenny 's contract at Toulon ends in summer 2016 , with Cardiff Blues reported to be interested in re - signing the player . The 26 - year - old left the Blues for France in the summer of 2014 . " He 's no different to anyone else . If he is serious about returning we 'd be interested to talk to him , " said Pivac . " We do n't have an endless budget , but I 've said it earlier and nothing has changed . " Pivac 's comments underline the financial realities faced by Welsh regional rugby . While the prospect of welcoming back a player of Halfpenny 's calibre is undoubtedly enticing for the Cardiff Blues , any potential deal would have to fit within the stringent fiscal parameters set by the region . This implies that Halfpenny , who commands one of the highest salaries in European rugby at Toulon , would almost certainly need to accept a significant pay cut to facilitate a move back to the Arms Park . His current deal with the French giants is understood to be in the region of £600,000 to £700,000 per season , a figure far beyond what any Welsh region could realistically afford .

The Wales and British & Irish Lions full-back has been a revelation since joining Toulon , quickly establishing himself as a key figure in their star-studded line-up . His formidable goal-kicking , defensive prowess , and courageous play have made him indispensable for the Top 14 and European champions . However , a serious knee injury sustained during a Rugby World Cup warm-up game in September 2015 has kept him sidelined for the majority of the current season , raising questions about his immediate future and recovery . Despite this setback , his market value remains incredibly high , and Toulon are reportedly keen to retain his services , offering a lucrative new contract . The decision for Halfpenny will likely come down to a choice between the high-octane , financially rewarding world of French club rugby and the potential pull of returning home to Wales , perhaps with an eye on the 2019 World Cup and the desire to be closer to family .

For the Cardiff Blues , a return for Halfpenny would be a massive coup , both on and off the field . He would bring a wealth of experience , a world-class kicking game , and an undeniable attacking threat from full-back . More importantly , his presence would provide a huge boost to the region's profile and commercial appeal , potentially attracting more fans to games and increasing sponsorship opportunities . Pivac has consistently emphasised the need for the Blues to build a squad based on a strong Welsh core , supplemented by key international talent . Halfpenny would perfectly fit this mould , having come through the Blues' academy system before making his name as a senior international .

The challenge for the Blues hierarchy will be to present a compelling case to Halfpenny that transcends purely financial considerations . They would need to highlight the chance to play regular rugby in Wales , to be a central figure in a rebuilding project at the Arms Park , and the opportunity to spend more time within the Welsh national squad environment – something that can be more challenging for players based abroad . While other Welsh regions , particularly the Ospreys , might also express an interest should Halfpenny choose to return to Wales , the Cardiff Blues would likely hold a significant advantage given his historical ties and affinity for the club where he began his professional career . The coming months will be crucial as Halfpenny weighs up his options , and the rugby world watches to see where one of the game's most sought-after players will ply his trade beyond 2016 . The dialogue between the player and the Blues , as alluded to by Pivac , will be central to determining whether a homecoming is truly on the cards for the Gwent-born star .

The Arsenal FC midfielder , 24 , uploaded a picture from his 2014 wedding with the caption " un flwyddyn heddiw " , which means " one year [ ago ] today " . In contrast to positive responses , some users expressed confusion while others ridiculed the message . One questioned whether the FA Cup winner was " drunk " The confusion stemmed from a misunderstanding of the Welsh phrase "un flwyddyn heddiw." While perfectly natural and idiomatic Welsh for marking an anniversary – meaning "one year today" – many English-speaking social media users interpreted it literally, failing to grasp its linguistic nuance. Aaron Ramsey, a proud Welshman, had posted the picture from his 2014 wedding on what was clearly his first anniversary in 2015. However, some users assumed the caption meant the picture itself was exactly one year old, which made no sense for a 2014 wedding photo. Others simply couldn't reconcile a 2014 event with a "one year today" caption, leading them to believe the FA Cup winner was confused about his own wedding date.

The decision by Mr. Ramsey to use his native tongue, a common practice for the midfielder, was widely misinterpreted. One Twitter user, @rightjudgeiam, sarcastically tweeted, "Does Aaron Ramsey not know how long a year is? 2014 wedding, posts 'one year today'. Welsh or not, that's just bad maths." This reaction highlighted a lack of understanding regarding the traditional use of such anniversary greetings in Welsh culture. The ridicule often stemmed from assumptions that he was implying the 2014 wedding had only happened "one year today" relative to the 2015 post. This episode underscored the pitfalls of social media, where context, linguistic differences, and cultural nuances are easily lost, turning an innocent, culturally specific message into a subject of online amusement and mockery.

The study tracked more than 200,000 Australian smokers and non - smokers above the age of 45 over six years . Mortality risk went up with cigarette use , BMC Medicine reports . Smoking 10 cigarettes a day doubled the risk , while 20 - a - day smokers were four to five times more likely to die . Although someone who smokes could lead a long life , their habit makes this less likely . Smoking increases the risk of a multitude of health problems, including various cancers, cardiovascular diseases, and respiratory illnesses. The study, published in BMC Medicine, underscored the profound impact of even moderate smoking on mortality rates, reinforcing decades of research on the dangers of tobacco. Lung cancer is perhaps the most well-known consequence, but smoking also significantly elevates the risk of cancers of the throat, mouth, oesophagus, bladder, kidney, pancreas, stomach, and cervix, as well as acute myeloid leukaemia. Beyond cancer, smokers are at a much higher risk of heart attacks, strokes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), emphysema, and bronchitis. It also contributes to conditions like type 2 diabetes, age-related macular degeneration (leading to blindness), and osteoporosis, weakening bones.

Prof Emily Banks, a leading researcher involved in the BMC Medicine study, emphasised that "Even smoking a few cigarettes a day has substantial effects on mortality." Her work, along with findings from other major health organisations, consistently points to a clear dose-response relationship between cigarette use and adverse health outcomes. Organizations such as Cancer Research UK and the American Cancer Society have long championed public health campaigns to reduce smoking rates, highlighting the preventable nature of many tobacco-related diseases. In the UK, significant progress has been made in reducing smoking prevalence, but it remains a leading cause of premature death and illness. The message from health experts is clear: quitting smoking at any age can dramatically improve health prospects and extend life, reducing the heightened risks associated with continued tobacco use. Even for long-term smokers, quitting starts a process of healing and risk reduction that can add years to one's life and improve overall quality of health. The evidence is overwhelming: every cigarette takes a toll on the body, making the decision to quit one of the most beneficial steps an individual can take for their health and well-being.

Cancer Research UK currently advises that half of all long-term smokers eventually die from cancer or other smoking-related illnesses.
But recent evidence suggests the figure may be higher.
Newer studies in UK women, British doctors and American Cancer Society volunteers have put the figure at up to 67%, says Prof Emily Banks, lead author of the Australian study.
"We knew smoking was bad, but we now have direct independent evidence that confirms the disturbing findings that have been emerging internationally.
"Even with the very low rates of smoking that we have in Australia, we found that smokers have around threefold the risk of premature death of those who have never smoked. We also found smokers will die an estimated 10 years earlier than non-smokers," she said.
George Butterworth, tobacco policy manager at Cancer Research UK, said: "It's a real concern that the devastation caused by smoking may be even greater than we previously thought.
"Earlier research has shown, as a conservative estimate, one in two long-term smokers die from smoking-related diseases in the UK, but these new Australian figures show a higher risk.
"Smoking habits differ between Australia and the UK [in terms of] how much people smoke and the age they start, so we can't conclude that the two-in-three figure necessarily applies to the UK."
In Australia, about 13% of adults smoke. In the UK, the figure is about 20%.
Stopping smoking can bring a person's health risks back down.

Rehtaeh Parsons , 17 , of Nova Scotia , killed herself in April after being taunted over a photo of her alleged rape by four boys , her mother has said . Two 18 - year - old men were arrested on Thursday in connection with the photograph . The men , who have not been named , will be prosecuted in a juvenile court . " We hope that today 's arrests help the community to heal , " Royal Canadian Mounted Police ( RCMP ) Superintendent Roland Wells said at a press conference in Halifax on Thursday.

Superintendent Wells, who leads the Nova Scotia RCMP's support services, emphasized that the investigation is active and ongoing, urging anyone with further information to come forward. He thanked the public for their patience and assistance throughout the complex review process. The arrests mark a significant development in a case that has drawn national and international attention, sparking widespread outrage and a critical examination of Canada's laws regarding cyberbullying and the sharing of non-consensual intimate images.

The decision to make arrests followed an intensive re-examination of the case by the RCMP, initiated after the initial investigation by Halifax Regional Police had concluded without charges in February. This earlier outcome had been met with widespread condemnation from Rehtaeh's family, victim advocates, and the public, leading to a direct appeal to the Nova Scotia government for intervention. Premier Darrell Dexter had personally apologized to Rehtaeh’s mother, Leah Parsons, for the handling of the case and formally requested the RCMP to take over the investigation.

Leah Parsons has been a relentless advocate for justice for her daughter, using social media and media interviews to share Rehtaeh’s story and highlight the devastating consequences of online harassment. She has consistently called for stronger legal measures and a more compassionate approach from law enforcement and the justice system towards victims of sexual assault. Rehtaeh's story quickly became a symbol of the urgent need for action against online violence, triggering a national debate on consent, privacy, and the responsibilities of internet users and service providers.

The two individuals arrested face charges related to the distribution of an intimate image, which allegedly depicted Rehtaeh's sexual assault. Due to their age at the time of the alleged offense and the specifics of the Youth Criminal Justice Act, their names cannot be publicly disclosed. The prosecution in a juvenile court underscores the complexities of applying existing laws to new forms of digital crime.

The community in Nova Scotia, particularly in Halifax, has been deeply affected by Rehtaeh’s death, with numerous vigils, protests, and online campaigns demanding justice and systemic change. While the arrests bring a sense of relief to many, including Rehtaeh's family, the broader conversation about cyberbullying and supporting victims of sexual violence continues. The RCMP’s commitment to this ongoing investigation aims to provide closure for the family and reinforce that such acts will be pursued vigorously by law enforcement. This case has served as a stark reminder of the digital age's darker side and the collective responsibility to create a safer online environment.

The life - size bronze effigy of the Native American stands in Gravesend , Kent , where she died on her journey home to Virginia in 1617 . Historic England has renewed its Grade II listed status and updated details of her life and role in Transatlantic history , confirming the monument's significance in commemorating Pocahontas, known also as Matoaka. The statue, erected in 1958, serves as a poignant reminder of her brief but impactful time in England, where she was presented to King James I and Queen Anne. Her story embodies the early, complex interactions between European settlers and Native American communities, particularly her marriage to English tobacco planter John Rolfe, which was instrumental in a period of peace for the early Jamestown colony.

The updated Historic England listing now explicitly acknowledges her Algonquian heritage and the often-misrepresented narratives surrounding her life, highlighting the agency she exercised within challenging circumstances. This recognition underscores the effigy's importance not merely as a local landmark in Gravesend, Kent, but as a national symbol of a pivotal moment in global history. The Grade II listing ensures the continued preservation of this unique memorial, reflecting its special architectural and historical interest. It emphasizes her tragic death at a young age in Gravesend before she could return to her native Virginia, underscoring the profound human cost of early colonial expansion and intercultural exchange. The statue, therefore, invites contemplation on themes of cultural encounter, diplomacy, and the lasting legacy of those who bridged vastly different worlds.

Ninety - three of the retailer 's 125 stores will close , with the rest remaining open while buyers are sought . If administrator KPMG can not find buyers , the remaining stores will also shut . The chain employed 1,658 people . The chain was sold to Greybull Capital last year by supermarket Morrisons , which has said it would offer jobs to ex - My Local staff . It has struggled since being acquired by private equity firm Greybull Capital in September 2015. The chain, formerly Morrisons M Local, was sold off by the supermarket giant as part of a strategic shift away from smaller convenience formats to focus on its larger superstores. At the time of the sale, Morrisons provided significant financial support to Greybull Capital, including a loan of up to £25 million, to help stabilize the business and facilitate its turnaround. However, the investment proved insufficient to reverse its fortunes in an increasingly competitive market dominated by established players like Tesco Express and Sainsbury's Local, as well as discounters.

The challenges faced by the former Morrisons' M Local stores under Greybull Capital’s stewardship were multifaceted. High operating costs, coupled with intense price competition and shifts in consumer shopping habits, created a difficult trading environment. Despite efforts to rebrand and reposition the stores as ‘My Local’, aiming for a community-focused offering, the chain failed to gain significant traction or achieve sustainable profitability. The decision to appoint KPMG as administrators came after a period of intense financial pressure, leaving no viable path forward without significant restructuring.

KPMG's immediate priority has been to manage the closure of the 93 unprofitable stores and to seek buyers for the remaining 32. Sources close to the administration process indicate that finding a single buyer for the remaining portfolio might be challenging, suggesting that individual or smaller clusters of stores could be sold off to other retailers or convenience store operators. The closure process will unfortunately result in the loss of a significant number of the 1,658 jobs, though Morrisons' proactive offer to re-employ former My Local staff, where possible, provides some relief to those affected. This gesture by Morrisons highlights its ongoing commitment, having initially established the convenience arm and then divested it.

The collapse of My Local underscores the difficulties even established players face in the convenience sector. Citing employee confidentiality, they would not discuss specific details of Ms Lennon's case, but reaffirmed the decision followed a thorough investigation into her conduct, concluding that her actions constituted serious breaches of policy.

Kim Lennon, however, strongly refuted the MoJ’s narrative, asserting that the disciplinary charges against her were a deliberate attempt to discredit her and suppress vital information about the critical state of Lewes Prison. She told reporters that her complaints, made over an extended period, had consistently been met with insufficient action by management. She highlighted that the current measures by the Ministry of Justice were clearly insufficient to tackle the deep-rooted problems within the prison.

During and since his flying days, Mr Costain says he has often been asked if he was frightened during the war years.

"If you were attacked when you were flying a Spitfire during the war years, you turned hard into the attacking aircraft and they just couldn't get behind you! It was much more manoeuvrable than the German aircraft.
"I don't think we should ever forget what the Spitfire did for England. It was virtually England's saving grace."

Hank Costain , 88 , from Charminster , near Dorchester , first flew a Spitfire in 1942 , at the age of 19 . The maiden flight of the Supermarine Spitfire took place on 5 March 1936 , from Eastleigh Aerodrome , now Southampton Airport . Mr Costain described flying a Spitfire as " absolutely marvellous " . He said : " When you first got into the seat and opened the throttle it felt as if someone had given you a good kick up the backside. The roar of the Merlin engine was deafening, a symphony of power that vibrated through every fibre of the airframe, and indeed, through my very bones. It wasn't just a machine; it was an extension of yourself, a living, breathing entity that responded to every subtle command.

The Spitfire was incredibly responsive, light on the controls despite its formidable power. Once airborne, the world transformed. Below, the patchwork fields and familiar landmarks of Dorset shrunk into a vast, detailed map. Above, the sky was an endless canvas, and in that moment, you felt utterly free, completely at one with the machine and the elements. We’d practice aerobatics, pushing the limits, feeling the G-forces press us into our seats as we banked sharply or pulled up into a loop. There was a sense of incredible exhilaration, a rush that I don't think anything else could ever truly replicate.

He recounted his initial training with a mix of fondness and the stark realism of wartime preparation. “Learning to fly the Supermarine Spitfire wasn’t just about mastering controls; it was about understanding its character. Each one had its own quirks, its own personality. You had to respect it, and it would look after you.” He remembered the intense pressure, the long hours in the cockpit, and the relentless drills designed to turn young men into formidable combat pilots. The sheer speed and agility of the aircraft, especially compared to the training planes, was astounding. It was a revelation, a technological marvel that put Britain at the forefront of aerial warfare.

For Mr Costain, the Spitfire was more than just an aircraft; it was a symbol of an era, a machine that played a pivotal role in shaping the course of history. “It saved us, didn’t it?” he mused, his eyes distant as if replaying old memories. “It was the best fighter aircraft in the world, and we knew it. Every time you took off, you felt that immense responsibility, but also an incredible pride.” He often returns to airshows, his gaze fixed on the familiar silhouette of a Spitfire performing graceful loops and dives, a ghost of his youth soaring through the modern sky. The sound of its engine still brings a lump to his throat, a powerful echo of a time when courage and ingenuity defined a generation. Even now, decades later, the memory of those flights remains vividly etched in his mind, a testament to the profound impact that the Supermarine Spitfire had on his life and the lives of countless others.

Four men deny attempting to smuggle 35 people into Tilbury Docks , Essex . One man died in the container . Basildon Crown Court heard one defendant been caught in France with migrants in the back of his lorry 11 days before the Tilbury incident . Timothy Murphy from Londonderry was fined √Ç¬£5,000 in August . Prosecutor Michael Goodwin told the court that the 35 migrants, including 15 children, were discovered on August 16 last year inside a container on the MV Titania, which had arrived at Tilbury Docks from Zeebrugge, Belgium. Conditions within the sealed container were described as “inhumane and life-threatening,” with temperatures soaring and oxygen levels depleting rapidly during the 10-hour voyage. The court heard that the victims had been deliberately locked inside the unit.

Mr. Goodwin explained that port officials heard unusual noises coming from within the container. Upon opening it, they found terrified and struggling individuals, many suffering from severe dehydration and hyperthermia. Among them was Meet Singh, 47, from Afghanistan, who tragically died during the journey. A post-mortem examination concluded that his death was caused by a combination of dehydration and hyperthermia.

The prosecution alleges that the four defendants, Stephen McLaughlin, 31; Martin McGlinchey, 49; Christopher Murphy, 20; and Timothy Murphy, 33, all from Londonderry, were part of an organised criminal conspiracy to smuggle people into the UK for financial gain. Mr. Goodwin highlighted Timothy Murphy's previous conviction in France, where he was caught attempting to transport 15 migrants in his lorry. This incident, just days before the Tilbury tragedy, suggested a sophisticated and repeated enterprise.

The court heard evidence that the defendants had been in regular contact via burner phones, coordinating their movements leading up to the incident. CCTV footage and phone data linked them to the vehicle carrying the container and to locations near Zeebrugge. The prosecution argued that the defendants were fully aware of the dangerous conditions the migrants would endure and showed a callous disregard for human life.

All four defendants deny a charge of conspiracy to facilitate illegal entry into the UK and a charge of manslaughter in relation to Mr. Singh’s death. The trial at Basildon Crown Court is expected to last several weeks, with further evidence to be presented regarding the planning and execution of the smuggling operation and the role each defendant played. The focus remains on establishing the extent of their knowledge and involvement in this tragic event, which ultimately cost a man his life and put dozens of others in extreme peril at Tilbury Docks in Essex.

Treviso, who had been dominating, suddenly looked rattled, while Scarlets, buoyed by the miraculous defensive stop, found a new surge of energy. Lachlan returns to the Murdoch empire as co - chairman of News Corp and 21st Century Fox , having previously stood back to focus on his own businesses . Meanwhile , younger son James was appointed co - chief operating officer at 21st Century Fox . After the phone hacking scandal , which rocked the Murdoch empire and led to the closure of the News of the World, James Murdoch had faced intense scrutiny over his leadership at News International, the UK newspaper arm of News Corp. His reputation was significantly tarnished, and the controversy derailed 21st Century Fox's (then News Corporation's) bid to fully acquire BSkyB. This period was widely seen as a major crisis for the family business, leading ultimately to the dramatic split of the old News Corporation into two distinct entities: the new News Corp, housing the publishing assets, and 21st Century Fox, holding the more lucrative entertainment businesses. James's appointment as co-chief operating officer at 21st Century Fox, alongside his brother's elevated role, signaled a strategic shift by Rupert Murdoch to solidify the succession plan and perhaps rehabilitate James's image within the company's more profitable divisions. Despite the prior setbacks, the move demonstrated Rupert's enduring trust in his sons to steer the future of the vast media conglomerate, marking a crucial transition as Lachlan and James increasingly took on operational control, preparing for Rupert's eventual step back. The focus on entertainment under 21st Century Fox allowed for a clear demarcation from the historical issues associated with News Corp's beleaguered newspaper division, aiming to project a fresh, forward-looking image for the company's global media ambitions.

Ashley Broomhall trekked to the summit of 3,560 ft ( 1,085 m ) Snowdon in Snowdonia before tackling Ben Nevis . It took him seven hours to walk up and down the 4,406 ft ( 1,344 m ) Scottish peak near Fort William . On the way up he had a snowball fight with other walkers . He now plans to walk 3,208 ft ( 978 m ) Scafell Pike in the Lake District . Mr Broomhall , from Whitchurch in Shropshire , has been doing the walks to raise money for Cancer Research UK . He was inspired to take on the gruelling challenge after seeing the devastating impact of cancer on close friends and family members. He believes that every step he takes, and every pound he raises, contributes to vital research that could save lives in the future.

His ascent of Snowdon, the highest peak in Wales, provided a challenging start to his mountaineering endeavours, offering stunning views of Snowdonia National Park despite periods of cloud and wind. The subsequent climb of Ben Nevis, the UK's highest mountain, proved to be an even more demanding test of his physical and mental fortitude. He recounted battling the notoriously unpredictable Scottish weather conditions, which ranged from clear spells to biting winds and snow flurries, even in what is considered late spring. The impromptu snowball fight on Ben Nevis's upper slopes offered a brief, memorable moment of camaraderie and fun amidst the arduous trek, highlighting the shared spirit among those conquering the formidable peak near Fort William. The descent, often as challenging as the ascent, required intense concentration and resilience, but the thought of the critical cause kept him focused.

With two of the UK's three highest peaks now conquered, Mr Broomhall is eagerly anticipating his final challenge: Scafell Pike in the Lake District. Completing Scafell Pike will mark the culmination of his personal 'Three Peaks Challenge', an iconic feat that involves climbing the highest mountains in Scotland, England, and Wales within a set period. He understands that while Scafell Pike is the lowest of the three, it presents its own unique difficulties, including rugged terrain and potentially tricky navigation, especially if weather conditions are poor.

Ashley Broomhall has set a fundraising target of £1,500 for Cancer Research UK and has already made significant progress towards that goal, having raised over £900 through a combination of online donations and sponsorship from friends, family, and local businesses. He expressed immense gratitude for the generosity shown by his supporters so far. "The support I've received has been overwhelming," said Mr Broomhall. "Knowing that people are backing me and contributing to such an important cause really motivates me to keep going, even when the climbs get tough. Every single donation helps fund groundbreaking research into new treatments and ultimately, a cure." He hopes that by sharing his journey, he can encourage more people to donate or consider their own fundraising challenges. Donations to Ashley Broomhall's efforts can be made via his dedicated JustGiving page, which can be found by searching for his name or his specific challenge details online. He remains committed to his fundraising mission, aiming to help contribute to a future where cancer no longer devastates lives.

Pte Sean Benton was found dead at the Surrey barracks with five gunshot wounds in June 1995 , while on guard at a perimeter fence . Human rights group Liberty said the Attorney General had given his family consent to apply to the High Court . An earlier inquest recorded a verdict of suicide on the 20 - year - old soldier . The coroner at a second inquest on Pte Cheryl James , who died at Deepcut in 1995, concluded in 2016 that her death was not suicide but an 'unlawful killing', a landmark overturning of the original finding. Pte James was one of four young soldiers who died from gunshot wounds at the Princess Royal Barracks, Deepcut, in Surrey, between 1995 and 2002. The others were Private Geoff Gray, Private James Collinson, and Private Kevin Williams. All four deaths were initially ruled as suicides, leading to years of tenacious campaigning by their families, who consistently maintained that the circumstances surrounding their children's deaths were suspicious and that the original investigations were fundamentally flawed.

The tragic sequence of Deepcut deaths became a national scandal, shining a harsh light on welfare provisions, alleged bullying, and the duty of care within the British Army. Families, often supported by organisations such as Liberty, fought tirelessly to have the original inquest verdicts quashed and new inquiries launched, believing that vital evidence had been overlooked or mishandled. The case of Pte Cheryl James, in particular, gained renewed traction when her parents, Des and Doreen James, secured a fresh inquest following years of arduous legal battles. This second inquest heard compelling evidence of a pervasive culture of fear, harassment, and even alleged sexual exploitation at the barracks, which her family powerfully argued contributed directly to her death.

Similarly, the family of Pte Sean Benton, also found dead at the same Deepcut Barracks in Surrey, has long sought a new inquest into his death. His sister, Tracy Lewis, and other family members have consistently challenged the original suicide verdict, citing numerous inconsistencies in the evidence and a disturbing lack of proper investigation at the time. The recent consent granted by the Attorney General for Pte Benton's family to apply to the High Court for a fresh inquest underscores the profound and ongoing concerns about the integrity of the original inquiries into these tragic deaths.

These landmark cases, driven by the extraordinary persistence and courage of the bereaved families and their dedicated legal teams, have had a profound and lasting impact on the understanding of military deaths and the standards of investigation within the armed forces. They have critically highlighted the urgent need for independent oversight and a transparent justice process when service personnel die in non-combat circumstances. The re-examination of these deeply troubling cases, particularly through the High Court and subsequent new inquests, represents a pivotal moment in the collective quest for truth and accountability, offering a glimmer of hope for long-awaited closure to families who have endured decades of anguish and unanswered questions regarding the deaths of their loved ones at Deepcut and similar military establishments.

North Ronaldsay Primary School 's single classroom will be kept on standby from August as Teigan Scott , 12 , moves to secondary in Kirkwall . Orkney 's most northerly island only has a population of about 50 people . Orkney Islands Council said the school would be brought back into use if more families with young children moved to the island . The building is also used by community groups . Island residents have blamed poor transport links for the lack of young families . Teigan told the BBC she was "sad to leave North Ronaldsay Primary School but incredibly excited for the new opportunities and challenges awaiting her at secondary school in Kirkwall." She spoke warmly of her time at the tiny school, highlighting the unique experience of having her teacher's undivided attention and the deep bonds formed within the island's close-knit community. "It's been amazing growing up here," she said, "everyone looks out for each other. But I'm also ready for the next chapter and meeting lots of new people from different places."

Teigan's departure brings into sharp focus the precarious future of communities on Scotland's most remote islands. With no other primary-aged children currently residing on North Ronaldsay, the temporary closure of its school marks a significant moment for the island's approximately 50 inhabitants. The school is not merely an educational establishment; it serves as a vital social hub, hosting everything from community meetings and exercise classes to social events, making its educational dormancy a keenly felt loss. Its active presence has long been seen as a beacon for the island's long-term viability, signalling the potential for new families to settle.

Orkney Islands Council, while acknowledging the emotional aspect of the decision, emphasized that the standby arrangement was a pragmatic, fiscally responsible step in response to demographic realities. A spokesperson stated, "While it's always regrettable when a school ceases to have pupils attending, this allows us to maintain the building and its resources, ready to welcome pupils back as soon as the need arises. We remain committed to supporting all our island communities and actively exploring ways to encourage families to consider the unique lifestyle offered by places like North Ronaldsay." This situation reflects a wider pattern of rural depopulation across the Scottish islands, where factors like declining birth rates, an ageing population, and limited economic opportunities combine to create significant challenges for local authorities trying to sustain essential services.

The island residents' concerns about poor transport links frequently surface in discussions about attracting younger families. The infrequency and cost of ferry travel to mainland Orkney and Kirkwall are significant barriers, making access to employment, secondary education, and specialist services challenging. This isolation, while part of the island's unique appeal, can also deter those contemplating a permanent move with children. Despite these formidable hurdles, the spirit of North Ronaldsay remains resilient. Community initiatives and a deep connection to the island's heritage continue, with many hoping that strategic investments in digital connectivity and more affordable, regular transport might yet tip the balance. The ambition is to one day hear the joyous sounds of children's play once again echoing from North Ronaldsay Primary School, signalling a new chapter for this remote but determined community.

For the first time , MPs have agreed in a vote that we will begin the process of leaving the EU by the end of March . The government chief whip was seen with a massive grin after tonight 's vote . Remember ministers ' climbdown came with a clever kicker , persuading Labour to sign up to their timetable for triggering Article 50 without committing to very much in return The 'clever kicker' was the government’s commitment to publish a Brexit white paper and allow a parliamentary debate on the negotiating strategy before Article 50 is invoked. This strategic concession offered vital political cover for Labour MPs, particularly those representing pro-remain constituencies. It enabled them to vote for the timetable, framing their support as a push for parliamentary scrutiny rather than capitulation to Theresa May’s agenda. This allowed them to appease concerned constituents and avoid accusations of obstructing the democratic will.

For Theresa May, this parliamentary triumph is paramount. It solidifies her authority over the Brexit process, demonstrating her ability to command a Commons majority for her timeline. The chief whip’s satisfaction signalled successful navigation of perilous political currents, momentarily silencing critics. This outcome strengthens May’s hand for complex negotiations with the EU, reinforcing her narrative that the UK is united in its resolve to leave by the deadline. The focus now shifts decisively from the mechanism of triggering Article 50 to defining Britain's future relationship with Europe.

However, deep divisions persist. While Labour’s leadership found a pragmatic way through, many within the party and the broader remain camp remain uneasy. The white paper offers limited real parliamentary power over final Brexit terms. Pro-remain voices will undoubtedly intensify as the immense complexities of disentangling from the EU become clearer, especially regarding single market and customs union access. The coming months will severely test the government’s resolve and party cohesion as Brexit’s true impact unfolds. This vote merely concludes the first chapter, ushering in the far more challenging phase of withdrawal and negotiation.

She alerted police but was told it was a "non-emergency" so she waited an hour with the killer for an officer to come.
Ms Braiden told BBC Radio 5 Live: "By the time we got to the devil card he broke down and started crying.
"It's the first time I've dealt with murder before. It was a shock but you have to be professional and I needed to keep him calm."

After gaining the defendant's trust, Ms Braiden asked him whether she could go outside to call the police. He agreed.
She said: "I explained [to the 999 operator] I was a tarot reader and told her a man had confessed to murder.
"She told me it was a non-priority call and I needed to ring the non-emergency number.
"Unfortunately they didn't believe me, but I'm not surprised at that."
She said she then bought Randel-Hanson a drink from a shop next door and waited 55 minutes for police to arrive.
"I asked him if it was ok if I took notes... I took names, places, where he had been stabbed and where the body was," she said.
"I didn't ask him why, and to be fair I don't think he wanted to talk to me about that.
"We joked about the time it took the police to come.
"He was getting tense at that point as I was not only looking for police through the glass doors, he was as well."

Professor Duncan Wingham said the row had " put a smile " on people 's faces . But MPs asked if he would be made to " walk the plank " by ministers, who were perturbed by the public outcry and ridicule. Despite the clear poll outcome, the National Environment Research Council decided against naming its new £200 million polar research vessel RRS Boaty McBoatface.

Instead, it was named RRS Sir David Attenborough, a choice reflecting its serious scientific mission and vital role in understanding global environmental changes. This sparked widespread public anger and accusations that the NERC had disregarded the democratic will, leading to social media uproar over the perceived hypocrisy.

Prof Wingham, while facing scrutiny, defended the NERC's stance, arguing a more dignified name was essential for a vessel undertaking critical polar and climate research. In his resignation letter , the home shopping magnate said he had " come to believe that it would be useful and more effective for the broader 'Leave' campaign, and indeed the national interest, if I were to step aside from my current role. My decision is not taken lightly and stems from a growing conviction that the internal dynamics within our designated lead campaign, as sanctioned by the Electoral Commission, have unfortunately reached a point where they risk undermining our collective efforts. Despite tireless work and dedication from many individuals, the persistent internal feuding and divergent strategic approaches have, regrettably, become an increasingly debilitating distraction. These divisions, which I have previously highlighted, prevent the unified and forceful message that is absolutely essential if we are to convince the British public that a future outside the European Union is not only viable but preferable. The emergence of multiple, often competing, 'out' campaigns, exemplified by the participation of figures such as Labour MP Kate Hoey in an alternative platform, further fragments our message and dilutes the impact of the arguments for departure from the EU. While diversity of opinion is a hallmark of a healthy democracy, the current landscape within the 'Leave' movement risks confusing voters and playing into the hands of those who wish to remain. For the 'Leave' campaign to succeed, it requires absolute clarity of purpose, a laser-like focus on the core arguments for sovereignty and economic opportunity, and above all, a cohesive and disciplined leadership that speaks with one voice. It needs to be perceived by the public as a unified force, not a collection of warring factions. It is my earnest hope that by removing myself from the immediate leadership structure, it may create an opportunity for a renewed focus on unity and strategic coherence. My commitment to seeing Britain leave the European Union remains absolute, and I will continue to support the broader 'Leave' cause from outside this specific leadership role. I wish the campaign every success in the vital months ahead. The stakes for our nation are incredibly high, and it is imperative that the 'Leave' side presents an irrefutable case for a brighter, independent future for the United Kingdom.

The collection of images , along with medals and badges , will go on auction later in July . The find " is like a time capsule that sheds new light on the war " , auctioneer Charles Hanson said . The photos were taken by Robert Oliver , who survived the brutal realities of the Boer War, serving with distinction as a Royal Army Medical Corps sergeant. His collection, meticulously preserved, offers an unparalleled glimpse into the daily lives of soldiers, the harsh landscapes, and the stark realities of conflict that shaped the early 20th century. Among the items is his coveted Queen's Medal for South Africa, complete with multiple clasps, a testament to his bravery and presence in pivotal campaigns, including those in the Orange Free State. This remarkable archive not only documents his personal journey but also provides vital historical context to the operations of the British Empire during a period of immense geopolitical change. Charles Hanson emphasized that such a comprehensive and personal archive is exceedingly rare, offering historians and collectors a unique opportunity to connect directly with the past. Oliver’s images capture both the grim determination of the troops and unexpected moments of camaraderie and quiet reflection, far removed from the staged photographs often seen from that era. These candid shots, combined with his medals and personal effects, paint a vivid portrait of a man who witnessed history unfold and had the foresight to document it. The sheer depth of the collection, detailing everything from medical tents to troop movements across the veld, makes it an invaluable resource for understanding the human cost and strategic challenges faced by the British forces. It truly is, as Hanson stated, a time capsule, brimming with untold stories and forgotten perspectives that challenge existing narratives of the conflict. The auction is expected to draw international interest due to the rarity and historical significance of Oliver’s contributions to documenting one of the British Empire's most challenging conflicts.

This ambitious Dolphin Women's Institute project aimed to capture Braintree's unique character through miniature landmarks. Initiated during lockdowns, it offered members a creative outlet and shared goal. Led by talented Elaine Pye, a long-standing member and avid knitter, the group focused on iconic structures defining Braintree's heritage. Beyond the meticulously crafted church and museum, other notable additions include the historic town hall, vibrant market square, and a miniature old railway station, each brought to life with incredible detail. The intricate process involved members dedicating countless hours to knitting specific textures and colours for each building's facade, windows, and roofs. Completed knitted sections were then carefully cut and sewn onto prepared cores, ensuring a perfect fit and realistic appearance. Elaine Pye, known for her intricate textile art, guided the team through challenging aspects, sharing techniques and encouraging collaborative work. This dedication has resulted in a unique exhibition celebrating both the town's history and the incredible crafting skills within the Dolphin Women's Institute. The completed collection is set to be displayed at various community events and local venues across Braintree throughout the coming months, starting with an inaugural viewing at the Braintree Museum. This public display will allow residents and visitors alike to appreciate the intricate workmanship and recognise their beloved town in a brand new, whimsical format. The project has fostered community among WI members and generated considerable local interest, drawing praise for its originality and charm. The Dolphin Women's Institute hopes this unique collection will inspire others, serving as a delightful testament to their creativity and commitment to enriching local life. While primarily focused on Braintree, the project's success has even garnered attention from neighbouring WI groups, with some Hertfordshire members expressing interest in similar initiatives.

Members of Braintree's Dolphin Women's Institute (WI) have stitched some of the town's best-known landmarks including the church and museum.
Each model is about 45cm (18in) tall and was created using a polystyrene or cardboard core with knitting sewn on.
It took nine knitters seven months to complete the seven miniature buildings which will be displayed at the town's museum next month.
The group's vice-president, Elaine Pye, said the project was inspired by a similar one a relative had been involved in knitting in Hertfordshire.
"They knitted their own cottages, but we couldn't really do that so chose some of the town's beautiful iconic buildings," she said.
Mrs Pye put together the polystyrene structures and each knitter got to work, returning after two weeks with their latest knitted piece of church spire or pub frontage.
After much gluing, sewing and additional knitted embellishments, the town finally took shape, brought together with mini woollen market stalls.
The group created models of the town hall, church, Swan pub, library, museum, shopping centre and even the railway station complete with knitted train.
"It really brought everyone together and the response has been amazing," Mrs Pye said.
"So much so that they want to do more, so we think we might knit the Public Gardens next."

The deaths deepened political tensions in Paraguay and were used by congress to oust the left - wing President Fernando Lugo . Four men received sentences of between 18 and 30 years in jail This tragic incident, which unfolded on June 15, 2012, at the Campos Morumbi estate in Curuguaty, became widely known as the Curuguaty Massacre. The land in question was fiercely disputed, with landless farmers claiming it as state property intended for agrarian reform. The subsequent judicial process was highly controversial; human rights organizations and international observers heavily criticized the trial of the eleven farmers, alleging a lack of due process and insufficient evidence linking them to the police deaths.

The massacre provided the immediate catalyst for the Paraguayan congress to orchestrate a rapid impeachment of President Fernando Lugo. The killer stabbed him with the 25 in ( 63 cm ) serrated blade after leaping off a stolen moped , the Old Bailey heard . The 17 - year - old , who can not be named due to his age , was cleared of murder . He will be sentenced on 21 April . Mr Appleton , a popular and bright teenager, was an avid football fan and a beloved son and brother. His death sent shockwaves through the Islington community, leaving his family and friends devastated. He was described by those who knew him as a joyful and kind-hearted individual with a promising future ahead of him. The brutal nature of the attack, carried out in a public park, deeply rattled local residents and intensified concerns about knife crime among young people.

The Metropolitan Police launched a comprehensive investigation, meticulously gathering evidence and tracking down the perpetrator. Detectives worked tirelessly to piece together the events leading up to the fatal stabbing. The court heard how the assailant, riding a stolen moped, had pursued Stefan before cornering him in Nightingale Park, close to the area often referred to as the Red Pitch, a popular local recreation spot. The ferocity of the attack, involving a large serrated blade, was a key focus of the prosecution’s case.

During the trial at the Old Bailey, the prosecution argued that the defendant had demonstrated a clear intent to cause serious harm, if not death. However, the defence presented arguments challenging the specific intent required for a murder conviction, leading to the jury’s decision to clear the 17-year-old of murder, finding him guilty of manslaughter instead. This verdict, while acknowledging the defendant’s responsibility for Stefan’s death, has been met with mixed emotions by Stefan’s family, who had campaigned tirelessly for justice. They issued a statement expressing their profound grief and the permanent void left by Stefan’s passing, but also reiterated their commitment to advocating for an end to knife violence.

The sentencing hearing on 21 April will determine the consequences for the teenager who took Stefan’s life. The case has highlighted the urgent need for interventions to prevent similar tragedies and to address the root causes of youth violence in London. Stefan Appleton’s legacy, though tragically cut short, continues to serve as a poignant reminder of the devastating impact of knife crime on individuals, families, and communities like Islington.

The weapon was one of a pair of daggers discovered by British archaeologist Howard Carter in 1925 within the burial wrappings of the teenaged king . The origin of its unrusted iron blade has baffled scientists because such metalwork was rare in ancient Egypt . Tutankhamun was mummified more than 3,300 years ago . Italian and Egyptian researchers used " a non - invasive X - ray technique " to confirm that the iron blade was indeed of extraterrestrial origin, likely from a meteorite. The study, published in the journal Meteoritics and Planetary Science, analyzed the blade's elemental composition, revealing high levels of nickel and cobalt, elements typically found in iron meteorites but rare in terrestrial iron. This groundbreaking finding provided a definitive answer to a long-standing archaeological mystery that had puzzled experts since Howard Carter’s initial discovery of the dagger in Tutankhamun's tomb.

The sophisticated X-ray fluorescence analysis, conducted by researchers from the Polytechnic University of Milan and the Egyptian Museum in Cairo, eliminated any doubt about the blade's celestial source. The presence of nickel, in particular, was a key indicator, as iron extracted from ores on Earth rarely contains such high concentrations. This suggests that ancient Egyptian metallurgists, despite their advanced skills in working with gold and copper, utilized this unique, readily available raw material from the sky. The fact that the dagger has remained largely uncorroded for over three millennia further supports its meteoric origin, as meteoric iron is often more resistant to rust due to its unique crystalline structure and composition.

This discovery sheds new light on the technological capabilities and available resources in ancient Egypt during the New Kingdom period. It implies that the Egyptians were not only aware of falling 'sky-iron' but also possessed the skills to forge it into intricate objects of immense value, fit for a pharaoh like Tutankhamun. The cultural significance of such a material, literally descended from the heavens, would have been profound, adding to the mystique and power attributed to the young king. The other dagger found alongside it was made of gold, contrasting sharply with the 'celestial' iron one, highlighting the distinct and perhaps revered nature of the iron blade. This research emphasizes the interdisciplinary approach needed to unravel the secrets of ancient civilizations, combining archaeology, art history, and modern scientific analysis to provide unprecedented insights into the past of Tut and his people.

His decision to step away from the limelight, though temporary, allowed him to reconnect with his roots and find fresh inspiration, a move that has clearly paid dividends with this unprecedented chart dominance. The Official Charts Company confirmed that this double-top entry is a truly historic moment, reflecting the immense anticipation for new material from the globally adored singer-songwriter.

The two tracks, 'Shape of You' and 'Castle on the Hill', showcase different facets of Sheeran's musical artistry. 'Shape of You' is a catchy, rhythmic pop offering with a subtle dance influence, while 'Castle on the Hill' is a nostalgic, anthemic ode to his upbringing in Framlingham, Suffolk, capturing the essence of small-town life and youthful friendships. The contrasting styles demonstrate his versatility and broad appeal, ensuring both critical acclaim and commercial success. The immediate impact of both songs highlights the power of a well-executed comeback.

This phenomenal achievement comes amidst a highly competitive music landscape. While other artists like Drake have consistently dominated the charts in recent years with their own string of hits, Sheeran's simultaneous one-two punch is a unique feat that underscores his singular talent and dedicated fanbase. His return has undoubtedly revitalised the UK charts, bringing a fresh wave of excitement and setting a new benchmark for chart performance.

Upon hearing the news, Sheeran reiterated his gratitude to fans, acknowledging the hard work and personal significance behind both tracks. "It's been a long time coming," he remarked, referring to the creative process during his sabbatical. "To have both songs resonate so deeply with people, especially 'Castle on the Hill' which is so personal, means the world to me." The Official Charts Company added that the sheer volume of streams and downloads for both tracks was staggering, easily surpassing all other entries. This unparalleled success solidifies Sheeran's position as one of the most influential and popular musicians of his generation, proving that a hiatus can sometimes be the perfect catalyst for even greater triumphs. His ability to connect with listeners on such an intimate level, coupled with his undeniable songwriting prowess, continues to set him apart in the global music scene. Fans eagerly await further announcements regarding his forthcoming album, which is now poised to become one of the biggest releases of the year. The initial reception to these two singles suggests that his "gap year" has only amplified his creative output, leading to an even more refined and impactful sound. The music world is watching closely as Sheeran continues to break new ground and redefine chart history, demonstrating an enduring appeal that transcends genres and generations.

RamJam uploaded Southern Rail Tycoon on Thursday , and so far 45,000 people have played the tongue - in - cheek game . The aim is to stop guards from boarding trains , which leads to services being cancelled as profits are collected from passengers . It was inspired by months of cancellations due to an RMT dispute . Once a sufficient number of train guards board on a train and a delayed service eventually departs , the player loses the round, and is presented with a screen showing plummeting profits and irate pixelated commuters storming a virtual London Victoria station. The game, created by Brighton-based indie developer Tom Jackson, under his studio moniker RamJam, has rapidly become a viral sensation. Jackson, a long-time frustrated commuter on the Southern Rail network himself, explained the inspiration behind the satirical hit: 'I spent so many hours delayed on platforms, watching those departure boards mock me, that I just had to channel that frustration into something. It started as a joke among friends, but the more I worked on 'Southern Rail Tycoon', the more I realised how many people could relate to the sheer absurdity of it all.'

The game’s dark humour resonates deeply with those who have endured the real-life chaos on the network. Players must strategically deploy various humorous obstacles, from ‘broken signal’ alerts to ‘leaf on the line’ incidents, all designed to prevent guards from reaching their designated carriages. The more services cancelled, the higher the player's 'tycoon' score, reflecting their fictional mastery over the beleaguered railway. If too many services depart on time, or if guards successfully board multiple trains, the player's 'profit margin' collapses, leading to a swift game over.

Despite its cynical premise, Tom Jackson insists the game is not meant to be a serious political statement, but rather a cathartic outlet. 'It’s about making light of a difficult situation,' he stated. 'It’s satire. It’s a way for people to laugh at the chaos, rather than just fuming about it. We’ve had messages from people in London, Brighton, and all along the line saying how much they appreciate being able to turn their anger into amusement, even if it’s just for a few minutes.' RamJam is now considering updates to Southern Rail Tycoon, including new scenarios and 'disaster' events, as well as a potential mobile version, cementing its status as a cult classic for exasperated commuters everywhere.
