It was announced on Wednesday that the East Midlands Congenital Heart Centre , at Glenfield Hospital , was to stop children 's surgery services . It was one of 10 units under review nationally with the intention to focus expertise in fewer locations . The charity Heartlink said it would not accept the judgement . A spokesman for the charity , John Rigby , said : " We 're going to take stock , listen to what our reps have said, and then we will plan our next steps. This is absolutely not the end of the fight for the East Midlands Congenital Heart Centre. We believe this decision is flawed and will ultimately harm children and families across the UK. Heartlink will explore every avenue, including legal challenges and further campaigning, to reverse this damaging judgement."

This decision, part of NHS England's 'Safe and Sustainable' review, aims to consolidate specialist services into fewer, larger centres to improve outcomes for children with complex congenital heart conditions. While proponents cite better surgical results and comprehensive care through concentrated expertise, opponents like Heartlink argue that closing established units, especially those with strong reputations, fragments care and increases travel burden for families in regions like the East Midlands.

Glenfield Hospital's children's heart unit is also uniquely known for its Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation (ECMO) service, a vital life support system for failing hearts and lungs. It is one of only four paediatric ECMO centres in the UK. Though the ECMO service wasn't explicitly part of the surgical closure, clinicians and parents worry about the long-term viability of a specialist ECMO unit without a co-located surgical team. This interdependency is a core argument for campaigners like John Rigby, who fear that dismantling the surgical component will inevitably weaken or lead to the loss of the ECMO service, a crucial national resource. The future of specialist paediatric care in the UK is now under intense scrutiny, with questions raised about whether centralisation truly benefits all.

It was announced on Wednesday that the East Midlands Congenital Heart Centre, at Glenfield Hospital, was to stop children's surgery services.
It was one of 10 units under review nationally with the intention to focus expertise in fewer locations.
The charity Heartlink said it would not accept the judgement.
A spokesman for the charity, John Rigby, said: "We're going to take stock, listen to what our reps have to say and be guided by them. We're going to fight to do our very best to keep children's services here [at Glenfield]."
The centre, which conducts about 230 operations on children and 70 on adults each year, has the UK's largest ECMO unit (a form of partial cardiopulmonary bypass) which oxygenates blood of critically ill patients.
The unit will stop surgery for children but will remain open to diagnose patients and for monitoring and non-surgical treatment.
It serves a population of about five million, with the next nearest similar unit in Birmingham, about 40 miles (64.4km) away.
Leslie Hamilton, vice chair of the Safe and Sustainable review's steering group, said that as surgeons they felt surgical expertise was spread too thinly around the country.
He said: "We felt we had to concentrate the expertise and reduce the number of centres in the country so we could have bigger centres with bigger surgical teams.
"That would lead to sustainable care for the future and also a big improvement in care."

Data in its first call home since Tuesday 's flyby suggest the spacecraft experienced no upsets as it hurtled past the icy world at 14km / s ( 31,000 mph ) . The signal came through a giant dish in Madrid , Spain - part of a Nasa network of communications antennas . The message took four hours 25 minutes to traverse 4.7 billion km of space . The tension mounted as scientists and engineers at mission headquarters in Laurel , Maryland , waited for telemetry information . So there was joy and relief when the signal was finally confirmed to be robust and filled with precious data. A roar of applause erupted in the mission control room, followed by hugs and back-patting among the weary but elated team members. For years, this moment had been the culmination of relentless effort, meticulous planning, and countless sleepless nights. The successful transmission meant that the spacecraft, after its perilous close encounter, had survived intact and was now sending back the treasure trove of information it had collected.

The first packets of telemetry confirmed the health of all onboard instruments, including the high-resolution cameras, spectrometers, and magnetometers. Scientists immediately began processing the initial raw data, eager for the first glimpses of the mysterious icy world. This successful flyby represents a pivotal moment in our exploration of the outer solar system, pushing the boundaries of what is possible and offering an unprecedented look at a celestial body previously only dimly observed from afar. The data received promises to revolutionize our understanding of cryogenic geology, potential subsurface oceans, and the conditions necessary for habitability beyond Earth.

Mission scientists expect to be sifting through the downloaded information for months, if not years. Each byte of data carries the potential to unlock new secrets about the universe, from the composition of the ice to the potential presence of plumes or geological activity. The incredible journey of the spacecraft, travelling billions of kilometers from Earth, has now yielded its first major reward, validating the ingenuity of the engineers and the dedication of the scientists. This critical 'call home' was not just a technical triumph, but a profound affirmation of humanity's unyielding curiosity and its quest to explore the cosmos. The images and spectral data will provide a wealth of information about the surface features, atmospheric composition (if any), and magnetic field interactions, painting a comprehensive picture of this distant, enigmatic world. The mission team, having overcome the immediate hurdle of the flyby and data transmission, now faces the equally exciting challenge of interpreting what the spacecraft observed and translating those observations into groundbreaking discoveries. This initial success paves the way for deeper analysis and potentially future missions to similar targets, fueled by the insights gained from this remarkable encounter.

This divestment of its print media holdings, including the iconic Financial Times, signals a clear strategic pivot for Pearson. The company, under CEO John Fallon, is increasingly focusing on its global education business, aiming to streamline its portfolio and concentrate resources on digital learning and assessment tools. This marks the end of an era for Pearson as a diversified media conglomerate, aligning with a broader industry trend of specialization.

The potential sale of its 50% stake in the Economist Group, which publishes the influential weekly magazine, presents a more intricate challenge. Unlike the straightforward acquisition of the Financial Times by Japan's Nikkei, the Economist has a unique ownership structure designed to safeguard its editorial independence. A trust holds a significant portion of shares, and a consortium of long-standing family shareholders – including the Rothschilds, Cadburys, and Schroders, alongside Italy's powerful Agnelli family through their investment vehicle Exor – own the remaining stakes. John Elkann, chairman of Exor, had publicly expressed interest in increasing their shareholding, emphasizing their commitment to maintaining the publication's journalistic integrity and distinct ethos.

This inherent complexity, requiring consensus among existing shareholders deeply invested in the Economist's long-term vision, explains Pearson's cautious statement regarding "no certainty." For Pearson, completing these divestitures would solidify its identity as a pure-play education company, allowing it to dedicate all efforts to developing digital learning platforms globally and capitalize on the evolving education sector. These moves underscore the significant redefinition underway in the media and publishing industries.

The hashtag #IStandWithAhmed trended globally, highlighting concerns about overreactions and bias in school disciplinary actions.

For Mohamed El-Hassan Mohamed, Ahmed's father, the experience was deeply disturbing. He openly stated his belief that the school's actions were driven by discrimination and Islamophobia, prompting his decision to remove all his children from the local school system. Thrower was ordered to complete a 60 - day rehabilitation activity requirement, aimed at addressing his offending behaviour and preventing re-offending. As part of his sentence, he was also made the subject of a Sexual Harm Prevention Order (SHPO) for five years. This order imposes strict conditions, including restrictions on his use of internet-enabled devices and a prohibition on entering any public lavatories. Furthermore, Thrower was ordered to pay £2,500 in prosecution costs and a victim surcharge. The court heard details of how the Very Reverend Martin Thrower, who had served as the rector of Hadleigh in Suffolk for 15 years, had committed these offences. His reprehensible actions came to light when he was observed acting suspiciously at a shopping centre in Ipswich, specifically in the men's public toilets, leading to his arrest in August 2016. During the sentencing hearing at Norwich Crown Court, the presiding judge highlighted the profound breach of trust involved in Thrower's conduct, given his prominent and respected role within the Church of England and the local Hadleigh community. While acknowledging Thrower's early admission of guilt and expressions of remorse, the judge unequivocally underscored the seriousness of the voyeurism offences and the distress caused to his victims. The court took into account his previous good character and long service to the church as mitigating factors, which were instrumental in the decision to suspend his prison sentence for 24 months, but firmly emphasized the necessity for both punitive measures and active rehabilitation. The court heard that AJ suffered "catastrophic" injuries, including a lacerated heart and internal bleeding, consistent with a severe impact. Post-mortem examinations revealed that Ayeeshia Jane Smith also had historic injuries, including a previous brain bleed and fractures to her ribs, consistent with her having been subjected to non-accidental harm on more than one occasion before her death.

Opening the prosecution's case, Christopher Hotten QC told the jury that both Ms Smith, 23, and Matthew Rigby, 21, were responsible for the fatal injuries inflicted upon AJ. He alleged that the couple, who were in a volatile relationship, had engaged in a "joint enterprise" to inflict serious harm, or that one had caused the injuries while the other failed to protect the child. The jury was presented with evidence of a chaotic household where drug use, including cannabis, was prevalent. Ms Smith's admission about using her limited income support to fund drug purchases underlined the difficult environment AJ was living in. The prosecution highlighted texts and calls between Ms Smith and Rigby in the hours leading up to AJ's death, which painted a picture of tension and concern about AJ's health, specifically the worry that she may have ingested drugs.

During cross-examination, Ms Smith maintained her innocence, accusing Matthew Rigby of being the one who inflicted the fatal injuries. She claimed she had briefly left the room and returned to find AJ unresponsive. Conversely, Rigby's defence team argued that it was Ms Smith who was responsible, suggesting she had a history of losing her temper and being violent. The court heard conflicting accounts from both defendants, each attempting to shift blame onto the other. Social services had been involved with the family prior to AJ's death, and concerns about the child's welfare had been raised on multiple occasions. Evidence presented included records of these interventions and assessments. The trial, presided over by Mr Justice Haddon-Cave at Stafford Crown Court, continues to hear from medical experts, police officers, and other witnesses who were involved in the investigation. But Ruth Percival , 30 , said she had not seen him make any attempts to revive the baby . The inquest was halted in October when new medical evidence led the coroner to refer the case to prosecutors . In March , the Crown Prosecution Service said there remained " insufficient evidence to pursue a prosecution against anyone in connection with Jonathan's death. This decision meant that the coroner, Dr. James Adeley, could now resume the inquest into the circumstances surrounding the infant's passing. The hearing, which had initially begun in October of the previous year, aimed to establish the medical cause of death for Jonathan Percival, who was just 36 hours old when he died at the vicarage in Freckleton.

During earlier sessions, disturbing details had emerged, including the starkly contrasting accounts from James Percival and Ruth Percival. James Percival, who claimed to have delivered the baby, maintained that he had attempted to resuscitate the infant, performing mouth-to-mouth and chest compressions. He described the baby as being born "blue" and not breathing, prompting his immediate intervention. However, Ruth Percival, the child's mother, presented a vastly different narrative. She testified that she was in the room throughout the critical period and did not observe James Percival making any efforts to revive Jonathan. Her testimony cast serious doubt on his account of the events leading up to the baby's death.

The new medical evidence that prompted the coroner to involve prosecutors was not publicly detailed but was understood to have raised specific questions about the circumstances of Jonathan's death and the care he received. Despite this, the CPS concluded that the evidential threshold for criminal charges could not be met. The family of Jonathan Percival, including Ruth Percival, expressed their ongoing desire for a full understanding of what happened to the newborn. The resumed inquest was expected to hear further expert medical testimony and revisit the conflicting accounts from James Percival and Ruth Percival, with the coroner's ultimate goal being to provide a definitive conclusion on the cause and circumstances of Jonathan's tragic death in Freckleton, Lancashire. The legal proceedings continue to bring to light the complexities and emotional toll of the case for all involved, particularly the parents seeking answers.

Many felt the bombing was a direct consequence of Turkey's perceived inaction against Islamic State, particularly along its lengthy border with Syria, which has been a conduit for foreign fighters joining militant groups.

In the days that followed, Turkish security forces launched a series of nationwide raids, detaining hundreds of suspected militants from various groups, including alleged members of the Islamic State. The government stated that these operations were a comprehensive crackdown on terrorism, moving beyond just ISIS to target Kurdish separatist groups like the PKK as well. This broader approach, however, drew criticism from those who believed it was an attempt to deflect attention from the core issue of Islamic State infiltration and to suppress Kurdish political movements. The bombing in Suruc profoundly reshaped Turkey’s domestic security landscape and its foreign policy towards Syria, signalling a more direct and assertive, albeit complex, engagement in the fight against regional extremism.

" The Hungarian Mate came into the contest with an impressive record with 17 wins in his 22 previous fights , but it was evident from the first bell that Mate was in for a tough night. Taylor, known for his explosive power and intelligent boxing, wasted no time in asserting his dominance. He moved fluidly, cutting off the ring and landing sharp, accurate jabs that quickly reddened Mate’s face. The Edinburgh crowd, already buzzing with anticipation, roared with every connection. Taylor’s southpaw stance and powerful left hand proved particularly problematic for the Hungarian, who struggled to find his rhythm or land anything significant in return.

Within the first minute, a blistering combination from Taylor – a left hook followed by a straight right – sent Mate stumbling backward into the ropes. The Commonwealth gold medallist, sensing an early finish, pressed home his advantage with relentless aggression. Mate showed commendable resilience, trying to clinch and weather the storm, but Taylor's precision and volume of punches were overwhelming. Just past the midway point of the opening round, a perfectly timed left uppercut from Taylor snapped Mate’s head back, followed by a crunching right hook that sent the visitor to the canvas.

The referee immediately began his count as Mate struggled to regain his footing, his eyes glazed. Although he managed to clamber upright at the count of nine, his legs were clearly unsteady, and the referee wisely waved off the contest, deeming him unable to continue. The official time of the stoppage was just 2 minutes and 10 seconds of the first round, a truly emphatic and devastating performance from the Prestonpans pugilist. The packed Meadowbank Arena erupted in a deafening roar, a standing ovation for their hometown hero.

After the fight, a beaming Taylor soaked in the adulation of the crowd, acknowledging their support. Speaking to BBC Scotland later, he reflected on the win, reiterating his surprise at the swiftness of the victory. "I came here expecting a tough fight, maybe a few rounds to get warmed up, but I caught him clean early and just went for it. The support from the fans was incredible, it really spurred me on."

Manager Barry McGuigan, the legendary former world champion, watched on with immense satisfaction. "Josh showed tonight exactly why we believe he's destined for greatness," McGuigan told reporters. "His power, his speed, his ring intelligence – it's all there. He handled the pressure of fighting at Meadowbank in front of his home fans perfectly. This was a statement win, a clear message to the super-lightweight division. We're not rushing anything, as I said before, we've got to take the right fights at the right time to develop him properly. But he's learning and improving with every bout. We'll sit down, review this performance, and plan the next step. There are big fights out there for Josh, and he’s ready for the challenges that lie ahead. This performance only confirms that he is truly a very special talent, someone who could go all the way to the top of the sport." The victory marked another significant milestone in Taylor's rapidly ascending professional career, setting the stage for even bigger challenges and proving his pedigree on home soil against a credible opponent, even if the fight itself didn't last long. The buzz around Taylor grew exponentially after this dominant display at Meadowbank, solidifying his status as one of Scotland's most exciting boxing prospects, a true champion in the making, following in the footsteps of previous Commonwealth Games successes.

The Rhodesian Squadron Royal Air Force plane , based at RAF Wittering , crashed at Holme on 22 November 1940 . Pilot Officer Harold Penketh , from Brighton , did not bail out and died . The Spitfire remains were found after a geophysical survey of the area . It is hoped the recovered parts will be put on public display , offering a poignant reminder of the sacrifices made during World War Two.

Pilot Officer Penketh, aged just 20 at the time of the tragedy, was flying a Supermarine Spitfire Mk IIa, a crucial fighter aircraft during the Battle of Britain and its aftermath. While the exact cause of the crash remains unknown, it is speculated that he may have been attempting to steer his damaged aircraft away from the village of Holme, thus preventing further casualties on the ground, a common act of heroism among pilots of that era. His decision not to bail out, despite the clear danger, underscores the immense courage displayed by so many young men in the face of conflict. Harold Penketh's name is commemorated on the Brighton & Hove War Memorial, serving as a permanent tribute to his ultimate sacrifice.

The archaeological team, working closely with aviation historians and military experts, undertook a meticulous excavation following the successful geophysical survey. This state-of-the-art technique had revealed anomalies beneath the surface, consistent with buried metallic objects, leading them directly to the crash site. Over several weeks, a variety of artefacts were carefully unearthed, including fragments of the Spitfire's engine, sections of the fuselage, instrumentation, and personal effects believed to belong to Pilot Officer Penketh. Each piece recovered tells a part of the story, shedding light on the intensity of aerial combat and the grim reality faced by those defending the nation's skies.

The ongoing conservation efforts aim to stabilise and preserve these precious relics. Plans are underway to create an exhibit, potentially at a local museum or a dedicated aviation heritage centre, which will not only showcase the recovered Spitfire components but also tell the personal story of Harold Penketh and the wider context of the Rhodesian Squadron Royal Air Force's operations from RAF Wittering during the war. This display will serve as an educational resource, ensuring that the bravery of individuals like Penketh and the vital role of the Spitfire in Britain's defence are never forgotten. It will allow visitors to connect directly with a piece of history, understanding the profound human cost of freedom and the legacy of the young pilots who flew from bases like RAF Wittering. The community of Brighton, in particular, has expressed a deep interest in honouring one of their own through this significant historical recovery and memorial. The ultimate goal is to provide a fitting and lasting tribute to Pilot Officer Harold Penketh and all who served.

PwC 's annual survey shows that just 37 % think the economy will improve in 2015 , down from 44 % last year . Perhaps unsurprisingly , Russia 's bosses have gone from the most confident to the least , due to problems caused by sanctions and the falling oil price . In the UK , concern had risen sharply about the availability of talent . The number of chief executives concerned about the availability of key skills had risen sharply. This growing talent crunch in the UK, as revealed by the PwC survey, is seen as a significant threat to growth and competitiveness. Many UK businesses report struggling to find and retain staff with essential digital and technical competencies, leading to increased investment in upskilling existing workforces and a focus on attracting international talent where possible.

In contrast to the UK's talent focus, business leaders in Germany and France voiced different primary concerns. German CEOs, while relatively more optimistic than their French counterparts, were predominantly worried about global demand slowdowns and geopolitical instability impacting their export-heavy industries. The eurozone's tepid recovery also cast a shadow, with concerns over deflation and consumer spending remaining high. In France, chief executives were more preoccupied with domestic regulatory burdens and the need for structural reforms to stimulate economic activity. Confidence levels remained subdued across both nations, reflecting a cautious European outlook amidst ongoing economic uncertainties and the lingering effects of the debt crisis.

Globally, the PwC survey of over 1,300 CEOs highlighted a universal shift towards caution. Beyond Russia's unique challenges stemming from sanctions and falling oil prices, and the UK's specific talent woes, the overall sentiment was one of strategic retrenchment. Only 37% of chief executives globally expected economic improvement, down from 44%. This marked decline underscores a pervasive sense of uncertainty across various regions, influenced by factors ranging from commodity price volatility to geopolitical tensions. CEOs indicated a greater focus on operational efficiency, cost control, and organic growth strategies, with less appetite for aggressive expansion. Investment in innovation, particularly digital technologies, emerged as a key priority to build resilience and secure competitive advantage in a volatile global market.

Mencap and the Challenging Behaviour Foundation have spoken of the risks of moving patients hundreds of miles . The warning comes as the results of a serious case review into the abuse of patients at the private hospital near Bristol are due to be released . The abuse was uncovered during secret filming by the BBC Panorama programme . Eleven people have admitted charges of ill - treatment and neglect related to the abuse . South Gloucestershire Safeguarding Adults Board ( SAB ) commissioned the review , carried out by an independent investigator. The review meticulously examined the systemic failures allowing horrific abuse at Winterbourne View, the private hospital near Bristol. It delved into circumstances leading to patients being placed far from families and communities, a key concern highlighted by Mencap and the Challenging Behaviour Foundation. Their long-standing campaigns consistently warned against inherent risks of distant placements, which isolate vulnerable individuals, hinder family visits, and create environments where neglect and abuse are less likely to be detected.

The serious case review, commissioned by the SAB, sought to identify not only direct perpetrators but also broader institutional and commissioning failures. It scrutinised oversight mechanisms, or lack thereof, from local authorities and NHS trusts responsible for patient placement at Winterbourne View. Findings are expected to be stark, revealing how a system designed to protect vulnerable adults failed them catastrophically. The BBC Panorama exposé, using secret filming to uncover shocking abuse, served as a crucial catalyst, forcing a national reckoning with care quality for people with learning disabilities and challenging behaviour in residential settings.

The eleven individuals who admitted charges related to ill-treatment and neglect represent a tragic failure of individual responsibility, but the review's scope goes far beyond individual culpability. It aims to provide recommendations to prevent such atrocities. These are anticipated to include a significant shift away from large institutional placements towards smaller, community-based care closer to homes and families. Strong calls are likely for improved regulation, robust inspection regimes, and enhanced staff training. Furthermore, the review is expected to highlight the critical need for better communication between care providers, commissioning bodies, and families, ensuring concerns are heard and acted upon promptly.

Mencap and the Challenging Behaviour Foundation have advocated for comprehensive reform, pushing for person-centred care prioritizing individual rights, dignity, and access to a full life within their community. Their warnings about perils of out-of-area placements, often driven by lack of appropriate local provision or cost-saving, have been tragically vindicated by Winterbourne View. The SAB's commitment to releasing the full findings of this independent review demonstrates a crucial step towards transparency and accountability. Lessons from this harrowing episode must drive genuine, lasting change across health and social care sectors, ensuring safeguarding of vulnerable adults remains paramount. The imperative is to learn from systemic failures and implement robust measures to protect those who rely on specialist care, preventing any recurrence of neglect and abuse. The review's findings will undoubtedly inform national policy and practice, reinforcing the urgent need for a fundamental shift in how care is commissioned and delivered for individuals with complex needs, moving from isolated institutional settings towards inclusive, community-based support.

Campaign group Liberty says the powers , which are used by intelligence agencies to collect large volumes of data from electronic devices , amount to an " assault on our freedom " . The Investigatory Powers Act gained royal assent in November . The government has said it will defend the act . Powers covered by the act allow state agencies to control and alter electronic devices , read texts , online messages and emails, monitor phone calls and access location data. This controversial legislation, dubbed the 'Snooper's Charter' by critics, grants extensive surveillance capabilities to agencies like MI5, MI6, and GCHQ. Liberty, with director Martha Spurrier at the forefront, argues the act constitutes an "assault on our freedom" by enabling mass surveillance. Spurrier contends it permits indiscriminate data collection on ordinary citizens, setting a dangerous precedent for civil liberties rather than targeting specific threats. She calls it one of the most extreme surveillance laws in a democracy. Despite significant opposition, including from the House of Lords which sought stronger privacy protections, the Investigatory Powers Act gained royal assent. The government, under then-Prime Minister Theresa May, defended the act as vital for national security in the digital age. May argued it merely updated existing powers, bringing transparency and proper oversight through independent judicial commissioners. However, Liberty and other privacy advocates continue to challenge its proportionality. They highlight concerns over bulk data collection, device hacking, and the requirement for internet service providers to retain browsing history for 12 months, viewing these as unacceptable intrusions. Legal challenges are anticipated, potentially reaching the European Court of Human Rights. The act underscores a fundamental tension between state security and individual freedoms, with critics warning of a chilling effect on free expression.

Our devices and services transformation is progressing , " said boss Steve Ballmer in a statement . He added that Microsoft is launching a " wide range " of new products in the coming quarter . The report shed no light on who is to replace Mr Ballmer , who announced plans to retire within the next year. The lack of clarity regarding Mr Ballmer's successor cast a shadow over an otherwise positive earnings report. Investors and analysts alike are keenly watching the search for the next chief executive, a decision that will profoundly shape Microsoft's future direction. Speculation has been rife, with names from both inside and outside the company being floated, including former Skype president Tony Bates and Ford CEO Alan Mulally, though Microsoft has remained tight-lipped about the process. The transition comes at a pivotal time for the Redmond-based software giant as it strives to redefine itself beyond its traditional Windows and Office strongholds.

This "devices and services" push, championed by Steve Ballmer, represents a fundamental shift for Microsoft. It aims to integrate hardware and software more seamlessly, mirroring the successful strategies of competitors like Apple. However, the pivot has not been without its challenges. The reception to Windows 8, Microsoft's flagship operating system designed for touch-enabled devices, has been mixed since its launch, failing to significantly boost PC sales in a declining market. The acquisition of Nokia's devices and services division, a deal spearheaded by Mr Ballmer, is central to this strategy, promising Microsoft greater control over its smartphone ecosystem and a stronger competitive position in the mobile space. Analysts believe that the success of this transformation will largely depend on the new leadership's ability to execute on Ballmer's vision while also adapting to rapidly evolving consumer demands.

The promised "wide range" of new products likely includes further iterations of the Surface tablet, potentially a smaller version, and new smartphones under the Nokia brand. The next generation Xbox console, though already launched, will also continue to be a key revenue driver. Despite the positive earnings, some analysts remain cautious, highlighting the intense competition in both the enterprise and consumer markets. The departing Mr Ballmer leaves behind a company in the midst of a massive strategic overhaul, and the next CEO will face the immense task of accelerating this transformation while simultaneously rekindling investor confidence and innovating at a pace previously unseen at Microsoft. The coming quarters will be critical in determining whether Microsoft can truly shed its legacy image and emerge as a dominant force in the mobile-first, cloud-first world.

A total of 374 employees lost their jobs when Tullis Russell Papermakers , based at Markinch in Fife , went into administration in April 2015 . Each employee received the equivalent of eight weeks ' wages in compensation for their loss . The award follows a judgement from an employment tribunal in Dundee, handed down earlier this year. The tribunal's decision found that Tullis Russell Papermakers, a company with a rich history stretching back over 200 years in Markinch, Fife, had failed to properly consult its employees and their union representatives on the mass redundancies before the company's collapse. This failure to adhere to the statutory obligation for collective consultation under the Trade Union and Labour Relations (Consolidation) Act 1992, meant that workers were entitled to a protective award.

The case was spearheaded by former employees who sought justice for the abrupt and devastating job losses. David Martyn, a partner and specialist in employment law at the Dundee office of the law firm Gilson Gray LLP (formerly part of Bond Pearce, which was acquired), played a pivotal role in representing the affected workers. Martyn welcomed the tribunal’s finding, stating that it offered some measure of vindication and financial relief to the hundreds of individuals and families severely impacted by the mill's closure. He highlighted the importance of employers, even those facing insolvency, upholding their legal duties towards their workforce during redundancy processes.

The closure of Tullis Russell, a cornerstone of industry in Markinch and the wider Fife region, sent shockwaves through the community, marking the end of an era for papermaking in the area and leaving a significant void in the local economy. For the 374 employees, many of whom had dedicated decades of their working lives to the mill, the compensation, although limited to eight weeks' pay, provided essential support during a period of immense uncertainty and hardship. This protective award serves as a critical reminder of workers' rights during such challenging corporate transitions, ensuring that even in administration, companies are held accountable for their legal obligations concerning workforce redundancy.

GM's financial agony does not mean, of course, that Vauxhall and Opel will not prosper under their new owner.  Peugeot thinks it can squeeze ¬£1.5bn of savings out of the combined operation, and if it can help the French carmaker break into new markets the deal will have done its job.
GM, meanwhile, continues to shrink its ambitions and focus on the future. Since it was bailed out by the US government in the aftermath of the financial crisis, it has closed in America the Oldsmobile, Saturn, Hummer and Pontiac brands, and ditched its plants in Australia, where it had made cars since 1931.
This might be seen as a retreat from former glories, but it may instead reflect GM's hard-headed conviction that the future is China - where it is the strongest of the US players - and electric and self-driving cars, where America, not Europe, leads the way.

The fine print of the deal suggests something slightly different , and shows that GM has in fact taken a hit of up to ¬£6bn in order to get shot of Vauxhall and Opel . First , a big chunk of the price - three - quarters of a billion pounds - is not for car plants , but for loans taken out by the owners of Opel and Vauxhall This unusual arrangement highlights that rather than simply selling an asset, GM is effectively paying to divest itself of a long-standing financial burden. The bulk of the £6bn charge, however, stems from the substantial pension liabilities that GM has chosen to retain rather than offload to Peugeot. Estimates place GM's retention of pension obligations for Vauxhall and Opel employees at well over £5bn, reflecting the enormous cost of legacy commitments built up over decades. This decision, made in Detroit, underscores GM's strategic imperative to clear its balance sheet of European losses that have plagued its financial performance for years. By retaining these liabilities, GM avoids the potentially complex and protracted negotiations that would have been required to transfer them to Peugeot, thereby expediting the sale and providing a clean break.

The deal, therefore, is less about GM selling a profitable division and more about a costly exit from a market where it has struggled to compete consistently. For Peugeot, this acquisition of Vauxhall and Opel presents an opportunity to significantly increase its market share in Europe and achieve substantial economies of scale. However, it also means inheriting a business that has been unprofitable for nearly two decades, requiring significant restructuring and investment to turn around. The challenge for Peugeot will be to integrate the Vauxhall and Opel operations efficiently, streamline production, and reduce costs without alienating the workforce or diluting the brands' appeal. The focus for Vauxhall under its new ownership will be on platform sharing with Peugeot models, standardizing components, and rationalizing the product portfolio to improve profitability. This move signals a definitive shift in GM's global strategy, allowing it to concentrate resources on more lucrative markets like North America and China, and invest heavily in future technologies such as electric and autonomous vehicles. The severance of ties with Vauxhall and Opel frees up capital and management attention, enabling GM to pursue its growth ambitions elsewhere, even if the price of freedom came with a hefty £6bn cheque.

West Yorkshire Police confirmed last month that 16,000 tickets issued by police community support officers ( PCSO ) were not valid due because of an " administrative error " . But , the force said there was " no basis in law " for refunds , which would have " come from the public purse " . Many of the drivers paid the fines, unaware of the underlying error. The revelation sparked considerable public outcry and anger among those affected, who felt unfairly penalised by the West Yorkshire Police. Drivers expressed frustration that the force was acknowledging the invalidity of the tickets while simultaneously refusing any form of recompense. Legal experts weighed in, questioning the ethical implications of retaining funds collected unlawfully, even if there was no direct legal precedent for a refund. Some argued that while the law might not explicitly mandate refunds in such a unique administrative error scenario, the principle of unjust enrichment should apply, where one party should not benefit from another's loss caused by their own mistake.

The situation put the West Yorkshire Police under significant pressure to explain why such a fundamental error occurred and why transparency about the issue took so long. Critics pointed out that the public's trust in the police, particularly in the impartiality and correctness of their enforcement actions, could be severely damaged. The Police and Crime Commissioner for West Yorkshire acknowledged the serious nature of the administrative error and stated that a full internal review was underway to understand how the invalid tickets were issued by PCSOs for such an extended period without detection. This review aimed to identify weaknesses in the internal processes and implement robust measures to prevent a recurrence.

For the many individuals who had already paid their tickets, often under the threat of further penalties or points on their license, the news was a bitter pill. Some indicated they would explore avenues for collective legal action, seeking advice on whether a class-action lawsuit could compel the force to refund the monies. Consumer rights groups also got involved, advocating on behalf of the affected drivers and calling for a clearer legal framework to address situations where administrative errors by public bodies lead to financial detriment for citizens. The incident highlighted a significant loophole in the system, where a clear administrative blunder by the West Yorkshire Police left thousands of citizens out of pocket with seemingly no recourse, raising fundamental questions about accountability and citizen protection when dealing with official enforcement. The cost of individual legal challenges for the drivers would likely outweigh the value of the tickets, further complicating their options. The PCSO role and the scope of their powers were also re-examined in light of the incident.

On Monday , Mrs May met the first and deputy first ministers on a one - day visit to Northern Ireland . She stressed that no - one wanted a return to the " borders of the past " . Her meeting with Mr Kenny is understood to have focused on the impact of Brexit on British and Irish relations . Earlier in July , shortly after her appointment as the new prime minister , Mrs May spoke to Mr Kenny by telephone and agreed to build on the " strong, existing relationship" between their two countries. Mrs. May reiterated her pledge that there would be no return to the hard borders of the past, emphasizing the deep historical, cultural, and economic ties that bind the UK and Ireland. Her discussions in Belfast and Dublin were aimed at understanding the specific concerns of Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland, as both jurisdictions navigate the unprecedented challenge of Brexit. She acknowledged the unique circumstances of the island of Ireland, where the land border between the UK and the EU would present particular difficulties for trade, freedom of movement, and, crucially, for the delicate peace process established by the Good Friday Agreement.

During her meetings, Mrs. May assured all parties that the UK government was fully committed to protecting the peace agreement in all its dimensions. This commitment, she stressed, included finding practical solutions to the border issue that would respect the integrity of the UK internal market while avoiding any physical infrastructure or checks. She highlighted the need for flexible and imaginative approaches, signalling a willingness to explore innovative customs arrangements and regulatory alignment where necessary to prevent a disruptive outcome for the cross-border economy. The prime minister underscored the importance of ensuring that Northern Ireland’s unique position was reflected in the ongoing Brexit negotiations with the European Union, making it clear that the needs of Northern Ireland would be a priority for her government.

Mr. Kenny, for his part, conveyed Ireland’s significant concerns regarding the potential impact of Brexit, particularly the re-emergence of a hard border on the island. He stressed the importance of maintaining the Common Travel Area, protecting the rights of citizens, and safeguarding the integrated all-island economy, which has flourished since the peace agreement. Mr. Kenny reiterated Ireland's desire for a comprehensive and ambitious future relationship between the UK and the EU, one that would minimise disruption and uphold the principles of the Good Friday Agreement. He also emphasised the unique role of the Republic of Ireland as an EU member state, committed to the single market and customs union, yet also bound by its shared history and geography with the UK and Northern Ireland. Both leaders recognised that the challenges posed by Brexit required close cooperation and a pragmatic approach from all sides, including the European Commission and the remaining 27 EU member states.

The discussions also touched upon the broader implications for British-Irish relations beyond the immediate economic and political challenges. Mrs. May and Mr. Kenny committed to maintaining the strong bilateral dialogue and collaboration that has characterised their nations' relationship in recent decades. They agreed on the necessity of ongoing engagement at all levels – political, official, and civil society – to address the complex issues arising from the UK’s decision to leave the EU. The shared aim, they concluded, was to forge a new partnership that respects the referendum result while preserving the peace, prosperity, and close ties that have defined the relationship between the UK, Northern Ireland, and the Republic of Ireland, ensuring that the progress achieved since the Good Friday Agreement is not undermined by future arrangements. This joint determination to seek a pragmatic and mutually beneficial outcome underscored the significance of Mrs. May's visit as a crucial early step in shaping the post-Brexit landscape for the island of Ireland and for Anglo-Irish relations.

Chief Inspector of Prisons Peter Clarke published his findings following unannounced inspections . Challenges included staff shortages and increased use of new psychoactive substances , leading to more " unpredictable and violent behaviour " . But inspectors also found good staff - prisoner relationships and a " good range " of training and education . Despite safety declining since 2013 , Mr Clarke described it as a " mixed picture of progress throughout the prison estate. While some institutions demonstrated resilience and effective leadership, Peter Clarke's report highlighted a persistent struggle with systemic issues that continued to undermine the safe and effective operation of many establishments across England and Wales. The surge in violence, often linked directly to the ready availability of illicit drugs like spice, placed immense strain on both resources and the morale of dedicated staff.

A significant challenge identified by Clarke was the ongoing problem of staff retention. This issue, exacerbated by the demanding and often dangerous work environment, meant that many prisons struggled to deliver a full daily regime, leading to extended periods of lock-up for prisoners. Such reduced out-of-cell time often fueled frustration and further escalated tensions within already volatile environments. Crucially, the report by Clarke also drew attention to the critical issue of prison capacity. Many establishments were operating significantly above their certified normal accommodation. This widespread overcrowding, where cells designed for a single inmate were frequently housing two or even three, directly contributed to the documented decline in safety and the notable increase in violent incidents. It severely limited personal space, heightened friction between inmates, and made effective supervision considerably more difficult for staff.

Peter Clarke underscored the urgent need for sustained investment, not just in the physical infrastructure of prisons, but vitally in the recruitment, retention, and well-being of frontline staff. He emphasized that prioritizing the mental and physical health of both prisoners and staff was essential for creating environments truly conducive to rehabilitation, rather than merely containment. The Chief Inspector warned that without tackling these deep-seated structural issues, including the fundamental mismatch between the rising prison population and the available certified normal accommodation, the risk of further deterioration in safety and order within the nation's prisons remained unacceptably high. His findings provided a sobering assessment, urging the government to adopt a comprehensive and strategic approach to adequately resource and manage the future integrity of the entire prison system.

Logan Murdoch suffered serious injuries in the crash and was not breathing when the Great North Air Ambulance team arrived . Hayley Murdoch , 29 , and Sheila Dixon , 71 , both from Carlisle , died following the collision at Newby Cross in 2016 . Dr Laura Duffy called Logan , years after that harrowing day, to marvel at his incredible journey back to health. She vividly recalled the scene at Newby Cross, describing it as one of the most challenging she had ever encountered. Logan had been clinically dead, but through the swift, coordinated efforts of the emergency services – the first responders, paramedics, and the air ambulance crew – he was resuscitated at the roadside. He was then airlifted to the Royal Victoria Infirmary in Newcastle in a critical condition, placed in an induced coma, and remained there for several weeks, fighting for his life. His family, already reeling from the devastating loss of Hayley Murdoch and Sheila Dixon, braced themselves for the worst, enduring agonizing days and nights by his bedside.

Against all odds, Logan began a slow, arduous recovery. Dr Duffy recounted the initial prognosis, which had been bleak, suggesting severe brain damage and long-term disability were highly probable. Yet, Logan’s resilience and determination, coupled with exceptional medical care, defied these expectations. His rehabilitation was extensive, involving months of physiotherapy, speech therapy, and psychological support to help him come to terms with the traumatic event and the profound grief of losing his mother and grandmother. The call from Dr Duffy was a poignant reminder of how close he came to joining them. She told him that his survival was nothing short of miraculous, a testament to the life-saving work done in those critical moments at the crash site near Carlisle. Logan, now a vocal advocate for the Great North Air Ambulance, often reflects on that day, acknowledging that without their rapid response, he would not be here today to share his story or remember his beloved Hayley Murdoch and Sheila Dixon. The scars, both physical and emotional, remain, but so does an immense gratitude for the second chance at life he received.

On - loan Wolves man Adlene Guedioura went closest for the visitors, rattling the crossbar with a powerful long-range effort early in the second half. Despite their spirited efforts, Wolves struggled to find a way past Burnley's resolute defence, marshalled expertly by Ben Mee. The home side, buoyed by Rodriguez's brace, controlled much of the possession in the midfield, with Trippier continuing to be a menace down the right flank, his delivery a constant threat.

Burnley’s dominance was evident, and they continued to press for a third goal to put the game beyond doubt. Scott Arfield and George Boyd worked tirelessly on the wings, creating space for the full-backs to push forward. Trippier, in particular, seemed to be enjoying one of his most influential performances of the season, his crosses causing panic in the Wolves penalty area time and again. However, Wolves goalkeeper Carl Ikeme pulled off several key saves to deny Burnley further additions to the scoreline, including a superb stop from a fierce Rodriguez volley that would have completed his hat-trick.

As the game wore on, Wolves pushed higher, desperate to find a goal that would reignite their hopes. Garath McCleary, who had been involved in the early penalty incident, tried to make amends with some penetrating runs, but his efforts were largely isolated. Burnley’s backline, with Mee at its heart, stood firm against the late pressure. Manager Sean Dyche made tactical substitutions to shore up the midfield and defence, bringing on fresh legs to maintain their high work rate. The final whistle blew with Burnley securing a comfortable 2-0 victory, a result that reflected their superior attacking prowess and defensive solidity. Rodriguez's clinical finishing, combined with Kieran Trippier's exceptional service, proved to be the decisive factors in a commanding performance by the Clarets. The win saw Burnley climb further up the Championship table, consolidating their position as serious promotion contenders. Wolves, meanwhile, were left to ponder a missed opportunity on the road.
